description.narrative: A build-up of fiscal, macroeconomic and external imbalances and an unsustainable debt position culminated in an unprecedented economic crisis in Sri Lanka in 2022. Against the backdrop of dwindling concessional financing in the global fora, and Sri Lanka’s status as a lower middle-income country, access to financing is further limited. Sri Lanka’s external debt stood at 128% of its GDP at the end of 2022. Furthermore, UNDP data indicates that the highest contributor of Multidimensional Vulnerability is related to household debt-related vulnerabilities. Further, women and girls, in particular, bear the brunt of such disparities and suffer the most due to brunt of compounded discriminations resulting from crises, mainly due to entrenched gender roles, social norms and systemic barriers that limit their agency and access to resources, opportunities, and decision-making processes.This coupled with the country’s default status, existing fiscal constraints, and lack of proper budgetary allocations for sustainable development are continuing to be limiting factors, making investments toward sustainable development even more difficult. Owing to the compounding nature and differentiated impacts particularly on women, enhancing women’s access to financing also remains a priority. Against this backdrop, there are opportunities to put in place certain foundations to unlock sustainable financing. UNDP through the innovative financing portfolio is undertaking a two-fold approach to our financing interventions. This largely consists of planning – setting up the groundwork and the foundations for financing frameworks, and financing instruments, which collectively aim to promote an integrated approach to sustainable/innovating financing for sustainable growth (taking into account both public & private; domestic and foreign investments).
